description: Features learn their surfaces and dependencies, derivation proves formally whenever a finite model fits (including state machines with interleaving actors, and SMT when the space is too large), drivers run the application, action-sequence properties are evidenced, and reviewers see before/after snapshots of screens, contracts, data and examples per intent.
prose:
# Feature map, formal proofs whenever possible, and review with before/after snapshots

Lastro learns how a user reaches each feature, proves behavior formally whenever a finite model can express it
(including state machines whose actors interleave, as TLA+ model checking does, and with an SMT solver when the space is too large to enumerate), runs the application through its
surfaces, and shows the reviewer what changed next to the intents and verdicts: screens for the frontend, contracts,
data structures and examples of behavior for the backend. The engines stay the judges: Lastro never writes or fixes
application code, and its only AI steps stay intent extraction (with the survey that reads code) and proof
derivation. This proposal speaks of features, as the proposal that renames use cases to features does.

## The feature map

A feature may carry surfaces and dependencies. A surface says how a user or a client reaches the feature: its kind
(screen, route, command or api), a name in the user's words ("the left sidebar's chat list") and a locator the
driver understands (a URL path, a CLI command, an HTTP method and path, a selector). A dependency names another
feature this one needs to work (opening a chat depends on signing in). The extraction step proposes surfaces and
dependencies for every feature an intent adds, and for a feature an intent modifies it keeps the surfaces and
dependencies the feature already has, adding or removing only the ones the change calls for; the reviewer approves
them with the intent, like the description. A feature with no surface is not reachable by the driver and is listed as such.

`lastro map` prints the feature map: every feature with its surfaces, what it depends on and what depends on it. It
is deterministic. It rejects a dependency on a feature that does not exist or that was removed, and a dependency
cycle, naming the features in it. When a proposal changes a feature, the map lists the features that depend on it,
directly or not, as affected: their proofs and snapshots run again with the proposal's own.

For a repository whose features have no surfaces yet, `lastro bootstrap --surfaces` asks the survey step to read the
code and propose surfaces and dependencies for them. It writes a bootstrap proposal whose intents only add surfaces
and dependencies, never change a description, and that proposal is reviewed like any other.

## Formal whenever possible

The derive step must prove formally whenever it can. For each approved intent it first tries a finite model the
code can be checked against exhaustively: an input space of at most 100,000 points, or a state machine whose
reachable states number at most 100,000. When the space is larger, it tries an SMT proof (the clauses compiled to
SMT-LIB and checked by an SMT solver, by induction over the steps for a state machine). Only when neither can
express the intent does it fall back to sampling, traces or scenarios, and it then records why, in one of the reasons where proof stops or as a domain too
large to enumerate. The receipt counts how many intents are proved formally, evidenced, and beyond proof, with the
reason for each one that is not formal.

## State-machine proofs

A model may be a state machine: state variables with finite domains, an initial state, and events, each with finite
inputs. It may declare actors, several copies of the same process (two devices, three clients) that share part of
the state; their events interleave in every possible order, which is how races between them are found. The code
under proof is a step function from a state and an event (with the actor that raised it) to the next state.

Clauses are of three kinds: an invariant must hold in every reachable state; a step clause relates a state, an
event and the next state; a reachability clause says a state that satisfies a condition can be reached, which guards
the other clauses against proving nothing. When the reachable state space, across every interleaving, has at most
100,000 states, Lastro visits all of it breadth first, and a clause that holds everywhere it applies is proved, with
formal evidence and the number of states visited. A larger or unbounded space is not sampled first: if it can be proved, it is. Lastro tries an inductive proof
with the SMT solver (the invariant holds initially and every step preserves it), and a clause it proves this way is
proved, with formal evidence and the method named. Only when the solver cannot decide does Lastro explore by random
walks from the initial state with a fixed seed, and a clause that holds is then evidenced, never proved. A violation
comes back as the shortest sequence of events, each with its actor, from the initial state that reaches it. The TypeScript engine, the
Rust prover, the Go SDK and the .NET SDK visit the states in the same order and give the same verdicts and
counterexamples.

Every state-machine model is drawn as a statechart from the user's point of view: its states, the transitions
between them labelled with the events that cause them, each actor as a parallel region, and the states each invariant
forbids marked. The reviewer sees the statechart next to the intent's proofs and the counterexample path drawn on it,
and requests changes on the intent when the statechart does not match what they meant.

## Driving the application

Lastro drives the application through the protocols the market already uses, so any existing driver works. A web or
Electron surface is driven over W3C WebDriver (BiDi where the driver supports it), with any WebDriver server such
as chromedriver or geckodriver. An Android or iOS surface is driven over the same protocol through Appium. An api
surface is called over HTTP directly, and a command surface is run as a process. `.lastro/config.json` names, under
`drivers`, the WebDriver or Appium server and its capabilities, the HTTP base URL, or the command for each surface
kind. Only when no standard protocol fits does a driver speak Lastro's own JSON lines protocol: Lastro sends a
surface and a list of actions, and the driver answers with the observed state and the snapshots it took. Lastro
ships no browser or device of its own; the docs show a web setup, an Android and iOS setup with Appium, an HTTP setup
and a JSON lines driver.

A scenario is a list of steps, each an input and the output expected from it. For a screen the input is a user
action and the expected output is the observed state and, where layout matters, a reference screenshot; for an api
the input is a request and the expected output is the response, its status and its body; for a pure function it is
an input and an output of the model. A scenario that names a surface runs through its driver, each step's output is
checked against the expected one, and the result is empirical evidence; a reference screenshot matches when the share
of pixels changed stays under the tolerance the scenario sets. A driver that fails to start or times out fails the
scenario with the driver's error, never passes it. When a reviewer signs off an after screenshot, it becomes the
reference screenshot of that step for the regressions that follow.

## Properties over action sequences

A property-based check names a surface, the actions a user or client can take there and an invariant over the
observed state. Lastro generates action sequences with a fixed seed, runs each through the driver and checks the
invariant after every action. If it can be proved, it is: when the surface has a
state-machine model, the property is first checked over that model (exhaustively or by SMT induction) and is
proved there, and the action sequences then check that the running application follows the model. A property with
no model that holds on every sequence is evidenced, with the number of sequences and actions run and the
rule-of-three failure bound; it is never proved. A failing sequence is shortened to the shortest
prefix that still fails and then replayed once: if the replay does not fail, the check is reported as
nondeterministic instead of violated.

## Before and after snapshots

When a proposal is extracted, every intent gets a before snapshot of each feature it touches, taken on the current
code; when the proposal is proved, the same snapshot is taken on the new code and is the after. A snapshot has one
of four kinds, chosen by the feature's surfaces and models:

- screen: for a screen or route surface, the images the driver captured while running that surface's scenarios;
- contract: for an api or command surface, the contract the driver reports (the endpoint's or command's request and
  response shapes, as JSON Schema) and, for every feature, the model's inputs and outputs with their domains;
- data: the structure of the data the feature reads or writes, as the driver reports it (tables and columns, or a
  JSON Schema of a stored document);
- examples: a table of example inputs, the scenarios' inputs plus a fixed-seed sample of the model's inputs, each
  run on the before and the after code with both outputs side by side.

Each pair gets a deterministic comparison: for screens, the share of pixels changed; for contracts and data, a
structural diff that lists every field or column added, removed or changed in type, and marks a removal or a type
change as breaking; for examples, the rows whose output changed. An example whose output changed although no
approved intent's clause applies to its input is flagged as an unexpected change, and the proposal is not proved
while an unexpected change is not accepted by a reviewer.

Snapshots are kept with the documentation of the change, under the proposal, the feature and the intent that changed
it: `.lastro/docs/<proposal>/<feature>/<intent>/before|after/`. They are committed with the proposal, images included,
so every reviewer sees them in the pull request without taking them again; the proposal also records the SHA-256 of
each one, so anyone can take it again and see whether the result still matches. A snapshot of the whole repository
rather than of one feature lives in `.lastro/docs/<proposal>/repository/before|after/`.

An intent whose promise is a matter of human judgment (the layout looks right, the message is clear, the new error
response is helpful) stays beyond proof, but after the proof run it waits for a sign-off: a reviewer looks at its
before and after snapshots and signs it off or requests changes. A proposal is not proved while such an intent waits
for its sign-off.

## Reviewing the evidence

The review app shows, for each intent: the feature's place in the feature map (its surfaces, what it depends on and
what it affects), the statechart drawn from its state-machine model when it has one, its before snapshots during the
review and its before and after snapshots with their comparison after the proof run (images side by side for
screens, a diff for contracts and data, the changed rows for examples), and the verdict of every proof and property
with its counterexample. The receipt adds a Feature map section with the affected features, a state diagram in
Mermaid for every state-machine model, the formal coverage counts, the snapshots with their hashes and comparisons,
the unexpected changes and who accepted them, and the sign-offs with who gave them.

The CLI, the TypeScript, Go and .NET SDKs, the docs and the plugin's skills cover all of this, and the plugin's
review shows the snapshots' paths, the unexpected changes and the sign-offs still due.

useCases.name: Store use cases and proposals
useCases.before: The workspace keeps one file per entity: each use case in .lastro/usecases/<id>-<slug>.json (id, slug, name, description, history), each proof of a use case in .lastro/proof/<proof-id>-<slug>.json and each proposal in .lastro/proposals/<id>-<slug>.json, with its receipt next to it. Use cases are numbered UC-001, UC-002... and proposals P-001, P-002... with the next free number, never reused even after a removal; intents and proofs are numbered inside their proposal (P-007.I-03, P-007.PF-05) and keep that id when a proof moves to its use case; proofs derived straight from a use case are numbered inside it (UC-003.PF-01). Slugs are kebab-case and stable: a rename changes only the name. intents.json, spec.json and proof.json are no longer written. A use case file that still carries a proofs list is read as before, and its proofs move to .lastro/proof/ the next time the workspace writes that use case.
useCases.after: The workspace keeps one file per entity: each use case in .lastro/usecases/<id>-<slug>.json (id, slug, name, description, history), each proof of a use case in .lastro/proof/<proof-id>-<slug>.json and each proposal in .lastro/proposals/<id>-<slug>.json, with its receipt next to it. A use case file that still carries a proofs list is read as before, and its proofs move to .lastro/proof/ the next time the workspace writes that use case. useCases.name: Extract intents from prose
useCases.before: propose(prose, { submittedBy }) creates the next proposal file in .lastro/proposals/ with status open and sends the prose and the current use cases to an LLM through an AskJson transport with a fixed system prompt and JSON Schema (step "extract"). The answer lists intents, each the addition, removal or change of exactly one use case: id (P-n.I-nn), slug, name, a natural-language description of the change, change (add, modify or remove), the use case (an existing id, or a newly reserved id and slug for an add), a provability (formal, empirical, beyond-proof), a beyondProofReason ("none" or one of the five reasons) and a verbatim quote, and replaces: the existing proofs of that use case the new behavior contradicts, each with a reason (extraction receives every touched use case with its proofs in readable notation; for a remove the SDK lists every proof of the use case itself); one resulting use case per touched use case with its name and, for add and modify, the complete new description (after), all its intents combined, and the intents that produce it; decisions that reference intents by zero-based index; and notPromised items. The SDK fills each modify and remove with the use case's current description (before); the LLM never supplies it. The proposal (lastro: proposal/v1) records the baseline (sha256 over the canonical use cases without their proofs), the submitter, every intent proposed with no approvals, decisions D1, D2... with origin extraction, and the review policy. Intents have no kind. Without an LLM transport or a custom extractor, propose() throws.

When a proposal changes a feature, every feature that depends on it directly or transitively is listed as affected, and their proofs and snapshots run again with the proposal's own.

useCases.name: Bootstrap the feature map
useCases.after: lastro bootstrap --surfaces has the survey step read the code and propose surfaces and dependencies for the features that have none. It writes a bootstrap proposal whose intents only add surfaces and dependencies and never change a description, reviewed like any other proposal.

useCases.name: Derive the proof plan
useCases.before: derive(proposal) requires an approved proposal and asks the LLM (step "derive") with the models declared in .lastro/config.json, each touched use case's before and after with its approved and amended intents, the existing proofs of those use cases, each decision's question and answer (the chosen or else the recommended option) and notPromised. It writes pending proofs into the proposal, numbered P-n.PF-nn: each has a slug, name and description, the intent and use case it checks, the model and subject it runs against, and a check that is either a clause (requires and ensures in LSL, assumptions used) or a scenario (concrete input and an LSL expect); plus assumptions and beyondProof items. Every remove intent gets a proof, written from the use case's before, that the old behavior no longer happens; when the model cannot express it, derivation returns a decision for the reviewer and the proposal cannot be applied while it is open. Derivation never retires a proof: the proposal's supersedes is the union of replaces over the approved and amended intents, each new proof that takes the place of one lists it, and an existing proof the approved behavior breaks that no approved intent replaces comes back as a decision that sends the intent back to review with the proof added to its replaces. Every expression is parsed and validated. The proposal moves to proving. Without an LLM transport or a custom deriver, derive() throws.

It writes pending proofs into the proposal, numbered P-n.PF-nn: each has a slug, name and description, the intent and use case it checks, the model and subject it runs against, and a check that is either a clause (requires and ensures in LSL, assumptions used) or a scenario (concrete input and an LSL expect); plus assumptions and beyondProof items. Every remove intent gets a proof, written from the use case's before, that the old behavior no longer happens; when the model cannot express it, derivation returns a decision for the reviewer and the proposal cannot be applied while it is open. Derivation never retires a proof: the proposal's supersedes is the union of replaces over the approved and amended intents, each new proof that takes the place of one lists it, and an existing proof the approved behavior breaks that no approved intent replaces comes back as a decision that sends the intent back to review with the proof added to its replaces. For each approved intent the derive step first tries a finite model the code can be checked against exhaustively (an input space of at most 100,000 points, or a state machine with at most 100,000 reachable states), then an SMT proof (the clauses compiled to SMT-LIB and checked by an SMT solver, by induction over the steps for a state machine), and falls back to sampling, traces or scenarios only when neither can express the intent, recording why as a reason where proof stops or as a domain too large to enumerate. Every expression is parsed and validated. The proposal moves to proving. Without an LLM transport or a custom deriver, derive() throws.

useCases.name: Render a receipt
useCases.before: The receipt is Markdown for a pull request, written next to the proposal: the overall result and counts per verdict; the proposal and plan hashes; the Rust check with coverage, table digest and whether verdicts agree; the use-case diff, with each use case added, modified (before and after) or removed with the intents behind it, each replaced proof next to the proofs that take its place, each superseded proof that still passes, each regression and, after apply, the new baseline hash; a table of intents with verdict, evidence, confidence and what backs each; notes; each proof with verdict, evidence, method (exhaustive, samples with failure bound, traces), mutants killed, formal statement, counterexample, violating trace and notes; trusted pieces; where proof stops; not promised; and pending contradictions.
useCases.after: The receipt is Markdown for a pull request, written next to the proposal: the overall result and counts per verdict; the proposal and plan hashes; the Rust check with coverage, table digest and whether verdicts agree; the use-case diff, with each use case added, modified (before and after) or removed with the intents behind it, each replaced proof next to the proofs that take its place, each superseded proof that still passes, each regression and, after apply, the new baseline hash; a table of intents with verdict, evidence, confidence and what backs each; notes; each proof with verdict, evidence, method (exhaustive, samples with failure bound, traces), mutants killed, formal statement, counterexample, violating trace and notes; trusted pieces; where proof stops; not promised; pending contradictions; the count of intents proved formally, evidenced and beyond proof, with the reason for each one that is not formal; a Feature map section with the affected features; a Mermaid state diagram for every state-machine model; the snapshots with their hashes and comparisons; the unexpected changes and who accepted them; and the sign-offs with who gave them.

useCases.name: Declare the proof vocabulary
useCases.before: A model has a name, inputs and outputs, each a domain: bool, enum of strings or numbers, int with optional min and max, or string with optional examples; plus named defs (parameters and an LSL body). Bool, enum and bounded int domains are finite and enumerable in a fixed, sorted-key order; unbounded ints and strings are not. Facts supplied by trusted external pieces enter as inputs. A model with no outputs is rejected by plan validation.
useCases.after: A model has a name, inputs and outputs, each a domain: bool, enum of strings or numbers, int with optional min and max, or string with optional examples; plus named defs (parameters and an LSL body). Bool, enum and bounded int domains are finite and enumerable in a fixed, sorted-key order; unbounded ints and strings are not. Facts supplied by trusted external pieces enter as inputs. A model with no outputs is rejected by plan validation. A model may instead be a state machine: state variables with finite domains, an initial state and events, each with finite inputs, and optionally actors, several copies of one process that share part of the state; its subject is a step function from a state and an event, with the actor that raised it, to the next state.

useCases.name: Prove state machines
useCases.after: A state-machine model's clauses are invariants, which hold in every reachable state; step clauses, which relate a state, an event and the next state; and reachability clauses, which say a state satisfying a condition can be reached and guard the others against proving nothing. The events of its actors are explored in every possible interleaving. When the reachable state space across every interleaving has at most 100,000 states it is visited breadth first, and a clause that holds everywhere it applies is proved, with formal evidence and the number of states visited. A larger or unbounded space is first proved by SMT induction (the invariant holds initially and every step preserves it), which counts as proved with the method named; only when the solver cannot decide is it explored by random walks from the initial state with a fixed seed, and a clause that holds is then evidenced, never proved. A violation comes back as the shortest sequence of events, each with its actor, from the initial state that reaches it. Every state-machine model is drawn as a statechart from the user's point of view: states, transitions labelled with the events that cause them, each actor as a parallel region, and the states each invariant forbids marked, shown to the reviewer next to the intent's proofs with the counterexample path drawn on it.

useCases.name: Cross-check with an independent prover
useCases.before: With a Rust prover (lastro-core, loaded as WASM in TypeScript or run as the native lastro-prove binary from Go and .NET), prove() tabulates the code over the whole input space and the prover re-checks every clause from that table. The prover drops out-of-domain rows and counts missing inputs and nondeterministic rows (an input that appears with two different outputs). It calls coverage complete when every input of the space has a row and no row is nondeterministic or out of domain; an input repeated with the same output still counts as covered once. It says proved only with complete coverage, checks vacuity, mutants and consistency itself, and returns a SHA-256 digest of the table. The proof is ok only if the SDK report is ok, the prover is ok and both engines give every clause the same verdict.
useCases.after: With a Rust prover (lastro-core, loaded as WASM in TypeScript or run as the native lastro-prove binary from Go and .NET), prove() tabulates the code over the whole input space and the prover re-checks every clause from that table. The prover drops out-of-domain rows and counts missing inputs and nondeterministic rows (an input that appears with two different outputs). It calls coverage complete when every input of the space has a row and no row is nondeterministic or out of domain; an input repeated with the same output still counts as covered once. It says proved only with complete coverage, checks vacuity, mutants and consistency itself, and returns a SHA-256 digest of the table. The proof is ok only if the SDK report is ok, the prover is ok and both engines give every clause the same verdict. For state-machine models the TypeScript engine, the Rust prover, the Go SDK and the .NET SDK visit the states in the same order and give the same verdicts and counterexamples.

useCases.name: Drive the application
useCases.after: Lastro drives the application through market protocols: web and Electron surfaces over W3C WebDriver (BiDi where supported) with any WebDriver server, Android and iOS surfaces over the same protocol through Appium, api surfaces over HTTP and command surfaces as processes. .lastro/config.json names under drivers the WebDriver or Appium server and its capabilities, the HTTP base URL or the command per surface kind. Only when no standard protocol fits does a driver speak Lastro's JSON lines protocol: Lastro sends a surface and a list of actions and the driver answers with the observed state and the snapshots it took. Lastro ships no browser or device; the docs show a web setup, an Android and iOS setup with Appium, an HTTP setup and a JSON lines driver.

useCases.name: Run Given/When/Then scenarios
useCases.before: Each scenario runs the code on its concrete input and checks its LSL expectation over input and output. It passes or fails, with the output or the error; with no subject every scenario fails. Scenarios are empirical evidence, and assumptions list the scenarios that check them.
useCases.after: A scenario is a list of steps, each an input and the output expected from it: a user action with the expected observed state and, where layout matters, a reference screenshot for a screen; a request with the expected status and body for an api; a model input with its expected output for a pure function, checked by an LSL expectation. A scenario that names a surface runs through its driver; a reference screenshot matches when the share of pixels changed stays under the scenario's tolerance. It passes or fails, with the output or the error; with no subject every scenario fails, and a driver that fails to start or times out fails the scenario with the driver's error. When a reviewer signs off an after screenshot, it becomes the reference screenshot of that step for later regressions. Scenarios are empirical evidence, and assumptions list the scenarios that check them.

useCases.name: Check properties over action sequences
useCases.after: A property-based check names a surface, the actions a user or client can take there and an invariant over the observed state. Lastro generates action sequences with a fixed seed, runs each through the driver and checks the invariant after every action. When the surface has a state-machine model, the property is first checked over that model, exhaustively or by SMT induction, and proved there, and the sequences check that the running application follows the model; a property with no model that holds on every sequence is evidenced, with the number of sequences and actions run and the rule-of-three failure bound, never proved. A failing sequence is shortened to its shortest failing prefix and replayed once; if the replay does not fail, the check is reported as nondeterministic instead of violated.

useCases.name: Snapshot before and after
useCases.after: At extraction every intent gets a before snapshot of each feature it touches, taken on the current code; when the proposal is proved the same snapshot is taken on the new code as the after. A screen snapshot (screen or route surface) is the images the driver captured while running the surface's scenarios, compared as the share of pixels changed. A contract snapshot is the request and response shapes an api or command surface's driver reports as JSON Schema, plus every feature's model inputs and outputs with their domains. A data snapshot is the structure of the data the feature reads or writes (tables and columns, or a JSON Schema of a stored document). Contracts and data are compared by a deterministic structural diff listing every field or column added, removed or changed in type, a removal or type change marked breaking. An examples snapshot is a table of the scenarios' inputs plus a fixed-seed sample of the model's inputs, run on the before and after code with both outputs side by side; the comparison lists the rows whose output changed, and a changed row where no approved intent's clause applies is an unexpected change that must be accepted by a reviewer. Snapshots are kept in .lastro/docs/<proposal>/<feature>/<intent>/before|after/ and committed with the proposal, images included; a whole-repository snapshot lives in .lastro/docs/<proposal>/repository/before|after/; the proposal records each one's SHA-256.

useCases.name: Mark where proof stops
useCases.before: Beyond-proof items tie an intent to one of five reasons (external-code, world-facts, termination-timing, human-judgment, unstated) with a note. An intent with beyond-proof items and no useful clause gets the verdict beyond-proof, with notes and any passing scenarios as partial evidence. The receipt lists them under Where proof stops.
useCases.after: Beyond-proof items tie an intent to one of five reasons (external-code, world-facts, termination-timing, human-judgment, unstated) with a note. An intent with beyond-proof items and no useful clause gets the verdict beyond-proof, with notes and any passing scenarios as partial evidence. The receipt lists them under Where proof stops. After the proof run, an intent beyond proof for human judgment waits for a sign-off: a reviewer looks at its before and after snapshots and signs it off or requests changes.

useCases.name: Track a proposal's status
useCases.before: A proposal has one status: open while its review is pending; changes-requested while a reviewer has an open thread; approved once approval succeeds; proving once its proofs are derived; proved when every proof, new and regression, passes; applied once apply has synced the use cases; closed when it is abandoned. status lists the proposals with their status, and status <proposal> its pending items.
useCases.after: A proposal has one status: open while its review is pending; changes-requested while a reviewer has an open thread; approved once approval succeeds; proving once its proofs are derived; proved when every proof, new and regression, passes, no intent waits for a sign-off and every unexpected change is accepted (until then it stays proving); applied once apply has synced the use cases; closed when it is abandoned. status lists the proposals with their status, and status <proposal> its pending items.

useCases.name: Review the evidence per intent
useCases.after: For each intent the review app shows the feature's place in the feature map (its surfaces, what it depends on and what it affects), the statechart drawn from its state-machine model when it has one, its before snapshots during the review, its before and after snapshots with their comparison after the proof run (images side by side for screens, a diff for contracts and data, the changed rows for examples), and the verdict of every proof and property with its counterexample.

useCases.name: Use Lastro from TypeScript, .NET or Go
useCases.before: Three SDKs expose the same pipeline (propose against the use cases, review with threads, pending, derive, returnDecisions, prove with the regression run, apply, gap review) with the same entities (use case, proposal, intent, proof), wire format, canonical hashes, seeded sampling, verdicts, receipts and prompts. Cross-check tests compare the .NET and Go reports and hashes with the TypeScript SDK, and all three with the Rust prover, on the reference login and its planted bugs.

Cross-check tests compare the .NET and Go reports and hashes with the TypeScript SDK, and all three with the Rust prover, on the reference login and its planted bugs. Surfaces, the feature map, formal-first derivation with SMT, market-protocol drivers, state-machine proofs with actors, statecharts, action-sequence properties, snapshots, unexpected changes and sign-offs are in all three SDKs and the CLI, with the same files, hashes and verdicts, and the docs describe them.

useCases.name: Review an agent's proposal like a pull request
useCases.before: The plugin's propose skill has the agent write the change as prose in .lastro/proposals/<id>-<slug>.md, run lastro propose (answering handoffs itself), show the user the review the plugin renders as Markdown (the PostToolUse hook adds it to the agent's context after the first lastro command that shows a new or re-extracted proposal in a session, and a one-line summary after later ones; lastro-plugin.mjs review prints it), then ask the user every open decision and, per intent, shown with the existing proofs it replaces, approve, request changes (amend) or reject, recording only the user's answers with lastro review --as <user>, until lastro status is ready; then lastro derive writes the proposal's proofs. With a policy above one approval the board shows each intent's approvals out of the required number and the proposal waits for the other reviewers.

decisions.name: How many examples
decisions.question: How many fixed-seed model inputs go into the examples snapshot, besides the scenarios?

options.label: 200, configurable
options.consequence: Enough to catch most unexpected changes, small enough to read in review.

options.label: The whole space when it has at most 1,000 points
options.consequence: Small models show every row; larger ones fall back to 200.

decisions.name: Driver timeout
decisions.question: What is the driver timeout that fails a driven scenario?

options.label: 30 s per action, configurable
options.consequence: drivers.<name>.timeoutMs in config.json, default 30000 per action.

options.label: One limit per scenario
options.consequence: Long flows need one large number; a single slow action is harder to locate.

decisions.name: How many sign-offs
decisions.question: How many reviewers must sign off a human-judgment intent or accept an unexpected change?

options.label: The review policy's approvals
options.consequence: Same quorum as approving intents (review.approvals in config.json).

options.label: Always one
options.consequence: Faster, but a single reviewer can accept a change a policy of two would not.

proofs.name: A surface is accepted with a known kind, a name and a locator
proofs.description: A feature file is accepted exactly when it has no surface, or its surfaces have a kind of screen, route, command or api, a name and a locator; dependsOn never makes it invalid.
proofs.subject: feature_surfaces

proofs.name: A feature file without surfaces or dependsOn stays valid
proofs.description: A feature file written before surfaces existed, with neither surfaces nor dependsOn, is still accepted.
proofs.subject: feature_surfaces

proofs.name: A modify keeps the feature's surfaces and only adds or removes what the change names
proofs.description: For a modified feature the after has the existing surfaces plus the ones added minus the ones removed, and removing more than the feature has is refused.
proofs.subject: extract_surfaces

proofs.name: An added feature takes the surfaces the extraction proposed
proofs.description: For a feature an intent adds, the after carries exactly the surfaces and dependencies the extraction proposed.
proofs.subject: extract_surfaces

proofs.name: lastro map prints the same map every time
proofs.description: Printing the feature map twice over the same features gives the same output.
proofs.subject: feature_map

proofs.name: A feature with no surface is listed as not reachable
proofs.description: In a valid map a feature is listed as reachable by the driver exactly when it has a surface.
proofs.subject: feature_map

proofs.name: The map rejects unknown, removed and cyclic dependencies
proofs.description: The map is accepted exactly when no feature depends on an unknown or removed feature and the dependencies form no cycle.
proofs.subject: feature_map

proofs.name: A dependency cycle is reported with every feature in it
proofs.description: A cycle is reported exactly when A, B and C depend on each other in a ring, and the error names all three.
proofs.subject: feature_map

proofs.name: Every direct or transitive dependent of a changed feature is affected
proofs.description: With A depending on B, B on C and C on A as given, a feature is affected exactly when it depends, directly or through others, on the changed feature; the changed feature itself is not listed.
proofs.subject: feature_map

proofs.name: bootstrap --surfaces proposes only for features without surfaces
proofs.description: A feature gets a bootstrap intent exactly when it has no surfaces yet.
proofs.subject: bootstrap_surfaces

proofs.name: A bootstrap intent that changes a description is refused
proofs.description: A bootstrap --surfaces intent is accepted exactly when it adds a surface or dependency and does not touch the description, and every description is kept.
proofs.subject: bootstrap_surfaces

proofs.name: The surfaces bootstrap proposal waits for review
proofs.description: The bootstrap proposal starts open and is reviewed like any other.
proofs.subject: bootstrap_surfaces

proofs.name: A space of at most 100,000 points is checked exhaustively
proofs.description: When the input space or reachable states number at most 100,000, the clause is checked exhaustively: proved when it holds, violated otherwise, with no reason recorded.
proofs.subject: formal_first

proofs.name: A larger space is decided by the SMT solver when it can
proofs.description: When the space is too large and the solver proves or refutes the clause, the method is smt and the verdict is proved or violated accordingly.
proofs.subject: formal_first

proofs.name: Sampling is used only when neither works, records why, and never proves
proofs.description: When the space is too large and the solver cannot decide or express the clause, it is sampled, the reason is solver-unknown or not-expressible, and the verdict is never proved.
proofs.subject: formal_first

assumptions: The sampled subject's violation, when there is one, is dense enough for the fixed-seed sample to hit it.

proofs.name: The receipt counts formal, evidenced and beyond-proof intents with a reason for each non-formal one
proofs.description: The counts equal the number of intents proved formally, evidenced and beyond proof, and there is one reason per evidenced or beyond-proof intent.
proofs.subject: formal_coverage

proofs.name: A state-machine model is accepted exactly when it is finite
proofs.description: A state-machine model is accepted exactly when its state variables have finite domains, its initial state is in them and its events have finite inputs, with or without actors.
proofs.subject: sm_model

proofs.name: Interleaving the actors finds a lost update
proofs.description: A shared counter that actors increment by reading and then writing is violated exactly when two or more actors run without an atomic step, and the counterexample uses two actors.
proofs.subject: sm_interleave

proofs.name: Invariant, step and reachability clauses get the verdict their truth calls for
proofs.description: Over a state space small enough to visit, each kind of clause is proved when it holds (for a reachability clause, when the state is reached) and violated otherwise.
proofs.subject: sm_clauses

proofs.name: A small state space is visited breadth first and proves formally
proofs.description: When the reachable states number at most 100,000 the method is breadth-first search, every state is counted, and a clause that holds is proved with formal evidence.
proofs.subject: sm_clauses

proofs.name: A large space is proved by SMT induction when the solver decides
proofs.description: For an invariant or step clause over a space too large to visit, a solver that proves the induction gives proved with formal evidence and the smt-induction method named.
proofs.subject: sm_clauses

proofs.name: Random walks run only when the solver cannot decide, and never prove
proofs.description: For an invariant or step clause over a large space that the solver cannot decide, the method is random walks with a fixed seed and the verdict is never proved; a clause that holds is evidenced.
proofs.subject: sm_clauses

proofs.name: A violation comes back as the shortest event path with its actors
proofs.description: A violated invariant or step clause over a visited state space comes back with the shortest sequence of events from the initial state, each naming its actor.
proofs.subject: sm_clauses

proofs.name: The statechart draws actors as regions, marks forbidden states and the counterexample path
proofs.description: The statechart has one parallel region per actor, labels every transition with its event, marks the states an invariant forbids exactly when there are some, and draws the counterexample path exactly when there is one.
proofs.subject: statechart

proofs.name: Every engine gives the TypeScript verdict, states and counterexample
proofs.description: For correct and buggy state machines, the Rust prover, the Go SDK and the .NET SDK visit the same number of states and give the same verdicts and counterexamples as the TypeScript engine.
proofs.subject: sm_crosscheck

proofs.name: Each surface is driven over its market protocol
proofs.description: With a standard driver configured, web and Electron surfaces use WebDriver, Android and iOS use Appium, api surfaces use HTTP and command surfaces run as a process.
proofs.subject: driver_protocol

proofs.name: JSON lines is used only when a driver is configured for it, and nothing is driven without configuration
proofs.description: The protocol is JSON lines exactly when the configuration names a JSON lines driver, and none when no driver is configured.
proofs.subject: driver_protocol

proofs.name: No SDK bundles a browser and every driver setup is documented
proofs.description: No SDK package depends on a browser or device, and the docs have a web, an Appium, an HTTP and a JSON lines setup.
proofs.subject: shipped_drivers

proofs.name: A driven step passes when its output matches and its screenshot stays within tolerance
proofs.description: With a driver that runs, a scenario step passes exactly when its observed output matches the expected one and, for a screen step with a reference screenshot, the share of pixels changed is at most the tolerance; a pass counts as empirical evidence.
proofs.subject: driven_scenario

proofs.name: A driver that fails to start or times out fails the scenario with its error
proofs.description: When the driver fails to start or times out, the scenario fails with the driver's error and is never passed.
proofs.subject: driven_scenario

proofs.name: Action sequences are generated with a fixed seed
proofs.description: Running the same property-based check twice generates the same action sequences.
proofs.subject: action_property

proofs.name: A property with no model that holds on every sequence is evidenced
proofs.description: A property checked through the driver, with no state-machine model, that holds after every action of every sequence is evidenced with the rule-of-three bound.
proofs.subject: action_property

proofs.name: A property with a state-machine model is proved over the model when the application follows it
proofs.description: With a model, a property that holds over the model and on every driven sequence is proved formally; one that the model violates is violated.
proofs.subject: action_property

proofs.name: A property with no model is never proved
proofs.description: Without a model, a property that holds on every sequence is evidenced with the rule-of-three bound, never proved.
proofs.subject: action_property

proofs.name: A failing sequence is replayed: violated if it fails again, nondeterministic otherwise
proofs.description: When a driven sequence fails, the check is violated exactly when the replay of its shortened prefix fails again, and nondeterministic exactly when it does not.
proofs.subject: action_property

proofs.name: A failing sequence is shortened to its shortest failing prefix
proofs.description: A sequence that first fails at action k is shortened to its first k actions; one that never fails has no prefix.
proofs.subject: shrink_sequence

proofs.name: Snapshots are before at extraction and after at the proof run
proofs.description: A snapshot taken at extraction is a before snapshot, and one taken at the proof run is an after snapshot.
proofs.subject: snapshot_kinds

proofs.name: A screen or route surface gets a screen snapshot
proofs.description: A feature gets a screen snapshot exactly when its surface is a screen or a route.
proofs.subject: snapshot_kinds

proofs.name: An api or command surface, or a model, gets a contract snapshot
proofs.description: A feature gets a contract snapshot exactly when its surface is an api or a command, or it has a model.
proofs.subject: snapshot_kinds

proofs.name: A feature whose driver reports data gets a data snapshot
proofs.description: A feature gets a data snapshot exactly when its driver reports the structure of the data it reads or writes.
proofs.subject: snapshot_kinds

proofs.name: The structural diff names every added, removed or retyped field and marks breaking ones
proofs.description: A field present only after is added, present only before is removed, present in both with different types is a type change, and otherwise unchanged; removals and type changes are breaking.
proofs.subject: structural_diff

proofs.name: The examples cover the whole space up to 1,000 points and list the changed rows
proofs.description: The examples snapshot runs the whole model space when it has at most 1,000 points, and the comparison lists a row exactly when its output changed.
proofs.subject: examples_compare

proofs.name: A change no clause explains is unexpected and blocks until accepted
proofs.description: An example is an unexpected change exactly when its output changed and no approved clause applies to its input, and it blocks the proposal until the policy's number of reviewers accept it.
proofs.subject: examples_compare

proofs.name: Snapshots are written under .lastro/docs, committed and hashed
proofs.description: Every snapshot file lands in .lastro/docs/<proposal>/<feature>/<intent>/before|after/ (or repository/before|after/), is not ignored by git, and its recorded SHA-256 matches the file.
proofs.subject: snapshot_files

proofs.name: A passing run is proved only once sign-offs and acceptances are in
proofs.description: After an ok run where every proof passed, the proposal is changes-requested when a reviewer requested changes on a human-judgment intent, proved when every due sign-off and acceptance has the policy's number of reviewers, and proving otherwise.
proofs.subject: proved_gate

proofs.name: A proposal whose run failed or did not pass is never proved
proofs.description: Without an ok run where every proof passed, the proposal is not proved, whatever sign-offs it has.
proofs.subject: proved_gate

proofs.name: The review app shows each intent's map, statechart, snapshots, comparison and counterexamples
proofs.description: For each intent the review app shows its place in the feature map, the statechart when there is a model, the before snapshot, the after snapshot only after the proof run with the comparison for its kind, and a counterexample exactly when a verdict is violated.
proofs.subject: review_evidence

proofs.name: The receipt shows the map, the state diagrams, the snapshot hashes, acceptances and sign-offs
proofs.description: The receipt has a Feature map section exactly when features are affected, a Mermaid diagram exactly when there is a state-machine model, snapshot hashes exactly when there are snapshots, who accepted exactly when an unexpected change was accepted, and who signed off exactly when there is a sign-off.
proofs.subject: receipt_evidence

proofs.name: The Go and .NET SDKs produce the TypeScript map, statecharts, diffs, verdicts and snapshot hashes
proofs.description: For the same workspace, the Go and .NET SDKs give byte-identical feature maps, statecharts, structural diffs, verdicts and snapshot hashes to the TypeScript SDK.
proofs.subject: sdk_parity

proofs.name: The plugin's review lists snapshot paths, unexpected changes and sign-offs due
proofs.description: The plugin's review lists the snapshot paths exactly when there are snapshots, the unexpected changes exactly when there are some, and the sign-offs still due exactly when there are some.
proofs.subject: plugin_review_evidence

proofs.name: A signed-off after screenshot becomes the step's reference
proofs.description: A step's reference screenshot becomes its after screenshot exactly when a reviewer signed that screenshot off, whether or not it had a reference before.
proofs.subject: reference_screenshot
